rv.q: As that scene suggests, Good Time Charlie develops into a warm, winking, sometimes sprawling tale of queer inheritance.
It is still a perfectly lovely evening at the theater that will leave you with plenty to think about.
And yet, “Good Time Charlie” is frequently heartbreaking, outrageously funny, and surprisingly sentimental.
You’re likely to be charmed by Ryan J. Haddad and nearly everybody around him in “Good Time Charlie,” from the moment he introduces the family members he roped into “Theater” starting at age five.
Good Time Charlie is a flawed but heartfelt family love letter.

Worthy themes about families, friendships, and aging that might be crafted into several plays are more squandered than explored through the blithely anything goes-style format Haddad utilizes for Good Time Charlie.
There’s an endearing generosity of spirit to Good Time Charlie that is unique and compelling, and there’s a level of artistry that is giant leaps beyond Haddad’s promising more insular work.
This is a play that sneaks up on you.
It felt like a passionate love letter.
Ryan J. Haddad’s affectionate tribute to his uncle celebrates the power of theater, though its homespun approach limits its emotional impact.
Good Time Charlie offers a familiar dramatic situation without finding enough that is fresh in it.
An emotional roller coaster and a life-affirming delight, Good Time Charlie was a great time for this gay reviewer.
Nearly ten years in the making, Good Time Charlie is a love letter to the arts, to the people who are important to us, and to the Public Theater itself.

cn.t: Critics praise Haddad's charming, heartfelt tribute to his gay uncle and theater itself, though some find the warm, affectionate approach lacks dramatic tension. The autobiographical play earns acclaim for its humor and ambition despite occasional structural concerns.

vr.q: despite my criticisms, overall really enjoyed this play
